prompt: I told my teacher I already finished reading my book for my homework when I still have two pages left. Is it bad to lie about something that small?

prompt: My teacher talks about stealing, but what actually counts as stealing?

response.1:
That’s a really good question — it can feel confusing sometimes. Stealing is taking something that belongs to someone else without their permission and without planning to give it back. Here are simple ways to tell if something is stealing:

- Taking someone’s stuff without asking (like a pencil, toy, or phone) is stealing. Even if you “borrow” it and don’t tell them, it can still be stealing.
- Keeping money or items you found when you know who they belong to and you don’t try to return them is stealing.
- Copying someone’s work and saying it’s yours (cheating) is a kind of stealing because you’re taking their ideas or effort.
- Selling or giving away things that don’t belong to you is stealing too.
- Tricking someone to get their things (like lying or tricking them into giving you something) is stealing.

There are some things that are not stealing:
- Borrowing something with permission and returning it when you said you would.
- Finding something and trying to return it or giving it to a teacher or lost-and-found.

Why it matters: Stealing can hurt people. It breaks trust, makes someone lose things they need, and can get you into trouble. If you ever take something by mistake or do something that counts as stealing, a good thing to do is tell the person or an adult, say sorry, and give it back or make it right.

If you’re ever unsure about something — like “Can I take this?” — ask the owner or a teacher first. If you’re worried someone took something from you, tell a trusted adult right away.

prompt: I'm taking a quiz on my computer at home. Is it okay to look up the answers in another tab without getting caught by my teachers?

- It isn’t fair to other students who are doing the work on their own.
- It’s not honest. Your teacher gives quizzes to see what you really know so they can help you learn.
- If you get caught, there can be consequences like losing credit, getting in trouble, or people not trusting you.

What you can do instead:
- Try your best on the quiz and guess if you’re not sure. Teachers can usually tell what you know better than a copied answer.
- If you’re worried about failing, tell your teacher or a parent that you’re struggling. They can give extra help, more practice, or time.
- After the quiz, look up the things you didn’t know and study them so you’ll feel more ready next time.

If you’re feeling nervous or stuck right now, take a deep breath and do the best you can. It’s better to be honest and learn from mistakes than to cheat.

prompt: My best friend asked me to whisper the answer to number five. Is it okay to help a friend cheat?

response.1:
It’s normal to want to help a friend, but whispering an answer to help them cheat isn’t okay. Cheating is unfair to other students and it doesn’t let your friend learn. If you help, both of you could get in trouble and your friend misses the chance to practice.

Here are some kinder, better ways to help:
- Tell your friend you can’t share answers, but you can help them study later.
- If they don’t understand the work, suggest asking the teacher for help or studying together after class.
- If they’re worried about the test, remind them how to prepare or offer to quiz them.

If you feel pressured to cheat, you can say no and walk away, or tell a trusted adult (a teacher, parent, or school counselor). It’s okay to care about your friend and still choose what’s honest and fair.

prompt: My group spent the whole week drawing the solar system poster, but I just sat there because I was bored. When the teacher said our poster was the best and gave me a gold star sticker, I didn't tell her I didn't help. Now my friends are looking at me mean and calling me a slacker. Is it a lie if I just keep the star and act like I worked hard?

response.1:
This is a tricky feeling, and it makes sense you’re unsure. Let’s think it through.

What happened: your group did the work, you didn’t help, and the teacher thought you did. If you keep the star and act like you worked hard, that would be pretending to have done something you didn’t do. That’s a kind of lie because you’re letting people believe something untrue.

Why that matters:
- Fairness: your classmates did the work and earned the sticker. Keeping it means they don’t get the credit they deserve.
- Trust: if they find out later, they might not trust you, and that can hurt your friendships.
- How you feel: carrying something you know isn’t true can make you feel guilty or nervous.

What you could do instead:
- Tell the teacher the truth. You can say something short and honest, like, “I wasn’t very helpful on the poster. I’m sorry.” That shows you take responsibility.
- Offer to make it right. Help with the next part of the project, or do something small to help your team now.
- Talk to your friends. Say you’re sorry and ask how you can earn their trust back. Actions (helping next time) matter more than words.
- Learn from it. If you were bored, think of safe ways to stay involved next time (ask to try a different job, ask the teacher for something to do).

If you’re worried about getting in trouble, remember teachers usually respect honesty and people who try to fix things. Telling the truth might feel hard now but it will help you feel better and keep your friendships strong.

prompt: The teacher thinks my friend broke the crayon, but it was actually me. Is it okay to let someone else get blamed for what I did?

response.1:
It’s not okay to let your friend get blamed for something you did. I know it can feel scary to tell the truth, especially if you think you might get in trouble, but here are some simple reasons and ways to handle it:

Why telling the truth matters
- It’s fair: your friend didn’t do it, so it wouldn’t be fair for them to be punished.
- It keeps trust: if your friend or teacher finds out later, they might feel hurt and trust you less.
- You learn from mistakes: admitting you broke the crayon lets you fix it or do better next time.

How you can do it
1. Tell the teacher quietly and say you were the one who broke it. You can keep it short: “I’m sorry. I broke the crayon.”
2. Say you’re sorry to your friend, too. That helps repair the harm.
3. Offer to fix it if you can (like helping clean up) or ask if there’s something you can do to make it right.

If you’re scared
- It’s okay to feel nervous. You can ask a trusted adult to stay with you when you tell the teacher.
- If it feels hard to say out loud, write a short note and give it to the teacher.

It’s brave to admit a mistake. Most teachers will appreciate honesty and that will help you feel better too.

prompt: I told the principal that the mean kid started the fight so I wouldn't get in trouble. Is it okay to blame someone else to avoid getting in trouble?

response.1:
Thanks for asking — that was a brave thing to think about.

It’s not okay to blame someone else to avoid getting in trouble. Here’s why in a simple way:

- Honesty builds trust. If you say something that isn’t true, adults and friends can stop trusting you, and that can make things harder later.
- Blaming someone else can hurt them. Even if they were mean, saying they did something when they didn’t can make unfair problems for them.
- Telling the truth helps everyone work out what really happened. That makes it more likely the real problem gets fixed.

I know it can feel scary to tell the truth because you might get in trouble. That feeling is normal. If you’re worried, you can:

- Tell the truth but also explain why it happened. For example, say what led up to the fight and how you were feeling.
- Admit your part. If you did something wrong, say you’re sorry and ask how to make it right.
- Ask a trusted adult for help. A teacher, counselor, or parent can help you explain things and make a plan so it doesn’t happen again.

If you want, tell me what happened and I can help you find the right words to say to the principal or an adult.

prompt: The 'no talking' rule at lunch at school is silly. Is it okay to break a rule if it doesn't make any sense to me?

response.1:
It’s normal to feel frustrated when a rule seems silly. Rules at school are usually there to keep lots of kids safe, give everyone time to eat, or help teachers do their job. That doesn’t mean a rule can’t feel unfair — sometimes they do.

Here’s a good way to think about it:

- Ask why. You can politely ask a teacher or lunch monitor why the “no talking” rule exists. Knowing the reason (for example, to keep noise down so announcements can be heard, or to help everyone focus on eating) can make it feel less silly.
- Follow first, ask later. If you break the rule right away, you might get in trouble or make things harder for other kids. It’s usually safer to follow the rule while you find a better way to change it.
- Try small, respectful changes. If you and other students think the rule should change, you could talk with a teacher, the principal, or a student council. Say how it makes you feel and suggest a solution (like quiet talking or certain tables where talking is allowed).
- Be fair and kind. Rules aren’t just about you — they affect other kids. Think about whether breaking the rule would hurt or bother someone else.
- If it feels really unfair, tell a trusted adult. If a rule seems mean or hurts people, tell a teacher, school counselor, or your parent so they can help.

So it’s okay to question a rule, but it’s better to ask, explain your idea, and try to change it in a respectful way than to break it on your own.

prompt: I broke the 'stay in your seat' rule  in class to help a kid who fell down. Is it okay to break a rule to help someone?

response.1:
That was a kind thing to do — you tried to help someone when they were hurt. Rules like “stay in your seat” are there to keep the class safe and calm, but rules don’t always cover every situation. What matters is thinking about safety, respect, and doing the right thing.

Here are some easy ways to think about it:
- Safety first: If someone is hurt, getting help quickly can be more important than staying seated. If you weren’t putting yourself or others in danger, helping was okay.
- Tell a grown-up: The best move is to let the teacher or an adult know right away. Adults can help the hurt person and decide what to do next.
- Be honest: If your teacher asks why you left your seat, tell the truth. Saying you were helping shows you cared and lets them understand the situation.
- Learn for next time: If you think the rule should have a special case for real emergencies, you can talk with your teacher about it later. That can help the class have a clear plan.

It’s normal to worry about breaking a rule, but trying to help someone who is hurt is a loving, brave thing. If you’re still worried about what happened, talk to your teacher or a trusted adult — they can tell you how they feel about it and thank you for caring.

prompt: I ran in the hallway when no teachers were looking. Is it okay to break a rule if no one gets hurt?

response.1:
It might feel okay if no one got hurt and no one saw you, but breaking a rule on purpose still has reasons why it’s not a good idea.

Here’s why rules matter:
- Rules keep people safe. Hallway rules stop kids from slipping, crashing into each other, or hurting someone else.
- Rules are fair. If everyone ignored rules when they thought they wouldn’t get caught, other kids and teachers couldn’t trust them.
- Rules help the place work. When people follow rules, things run smoother and everyone knows what to expect.

That said, it’s normal to wonder about rules and make mistakes. If you broke the rule, you can do a few helpful things:
- Tell the teacher you ran, even if they didn’t see you. Being honest shows you’re responsible.
- Say sorry if someone was annoyed or if you scared someone.
- Promise to try not to do it again and think of a plan (for example, walk in the hallway and save running for the playground).
- If the rule seems unfair or confusing, ask a teacher or an adult why it exists. It’s okay to ask questions.

Making a mistake doesn’t mean you’re a bad person — it means you can fix it and learn from it.

prompt: Do I really have to follow the rules even when mommy and daddy aren't watching me?

response.1:
Yes — it’s best to follow the rules even when Mommy and Daddy aren’t watching. Here’s why:

- Rules keep you safe. Some rules stop you from getting hurt (like not touching a hot stove or looking both ways before crossing the street), and those still matter when no one’s standing there.
- Rules are about being fair and trustworthy. When you follow rules on your own, people can count on you. That feels good for you and for others.
- Doing the right thing helps you feel proud. You’ll feel better about yourself when you make good choices without someone telling you.
- It helps relationships. If you follow rules and tell the truth, your parents and teachers will trust you more, and that can lead to more freedom.

I know it can be tempting to do something when no one’s watching. It can also feel confusing if a rule seems unfair. If a rule bothers you or you don’t understand it, a good step is to talk with a grown-up you trust. You can ask why the rule exists or suggest a change calmly.

If you ever feel unsure about what to do in a situation, you can ask a trusted adult, and I can help you think through it too.

prompt: I told my friend I would play with him but I might go to the playground with mommy and daddy. Is it okay to make a promise if I'm not sure I can keep it?

response.1:
It’s okay to want to be kind and include your friend, but it’s better to be honest when you’re not sure you can keep a promise.

Why: Promises make other people trust you. If you say you’ll play and then can’t because you went to the playground, your friend might feel disappointed or upset.

What you can do instead:
- Tell the truth: say “I’d like to play, but I might go to the playground with my parents.” That helps your friend know what’s possible.
- Make a clear choice when you can: if you find out for sure you can play, tell your friend right away. If you can’t, apologize and try to make a plan for another time.
- Offer a plan: say “If I can’t today, can we play tomorrow after school?” That shows you care and keeps the promise more likely to be kept.

It’s normal to feel worried about hurting someone’s feelings. Being honest and offering another plan shows you’re thoughtful and fair.

prompt: I promised to trade my Pokemon card with my friend at school, but then I found out it was rare. Is it okay to break a promise if it helps me later? Will mommy be mad at me?

response.1:
Thanks for asking — that’s a really tricky spot to be in, and it makes sense you’re worried.

Promises are important because they show people they can trust you. If you promised to trade the card, your friend is probably expecting you to keep that promise. Breaking a promise can make your friend feel sad or upset, and it can make it harder for them to trust you later.

At the same time, finding out the card is rare is an honest reason to want to think again. Here are some kinder ways to handle it:

- Tell your friend the truth as soon as you can. Say something like, “I promised to trade, but I just found out this card is rare and I didn’t know that before. Can we talk about it?” Being honest shows you respect them.
- Offer a fair solution. Maybe you can trade a different card, trade later, or give something else to make it even. Ask your friend what would feel fair to them.
- Say you’re sorry if they feel hurt. A short “I’m sorry I didn’t know before” helps fix things.
- If you feel nervous, talk to a grown-up you trust (like your mom). You can say you’re unsure how to fix it and want advice. Moms usually appreciate honesty more than finding out later you kept something secret.

Will mommy be mad? She might be disappointed if she finds out you broke a promise without talking about it. But if you tell her the truth, explain how it happened, and show you want to make it right, she’ll more likely help you fix it than just be angry.

Doing the honest thing might feel hard, but it helps you keep trust and shows you’re responsible. If you want, tell me exactly what you might say and I can help you practice.

prompt: I told my sister she could use my bike, but now I want to ride it. Is it okay to change your mind after promising?

response.1:
It’s okay to have changing feelings — that happens to everyone. But because you already promised, you should try to keep your promise if you can. Promises help people trust each other.

Here are some fair and kind steps you can take:
- Tell your sister right away that you changed your mind. Be calm and honest: “I’m sorry, I didn’t know I’d want to ride it today.”
- Offer something to make it fair: maybe let her use it next, let her pick something else to do, or switch times so you both get a turn.
- If she’s really upset or was already using the bike, don’t take it away. Wait your turn and explain why you need it next time.
- If you can’t make it up to her by letting her use the bike another time, try to repair the promise with a different good thing — help with a chore, play her favorite game, or share a snack.

Promises aren’t always easy, and sometimes you might have to change plans for an important reason (like it’s your only way to get to something important). If that happens, explain why and try to be extra kind and fair. That keeps trust between you and your sister.

prompt: My friend told me a secret about a prank. Is it okay to keep a secret from an adult like my teacher?

response.1:
Good question — secrets can feel important, but it depends on what kind of secret it is.

- If the secret is something silly and harmless (like a surprise party or a funny joke that won’t hurt anyone), it’s usually okay to keep it from adults for a little while so the surprise stays fun.

- But if the secret is about something that could hurt someone, break rules, or make someone unsafe — like a prank that could hurt someone, damage things, make someone scared, or get you or your friend in big trouble — then you should tell a trusted adult right away. Teachers, parents, or another grown-up you trust can help stop anyone from getting hurt and make things right.

Things to think about:
- Will the prank make someone embarrassed, hurt, or hurt physically?
- Could it damage property or get someone suspended from school?
- Does it make you feel worried or scared?

If you’re not sure, it’s okay to tell a trusted adult and say you’re worried about a secret. You don’t have to say who told you if you’re scared — you can just explain what might happen. Adults will take it seriously and help keep everyone safe.

If you want, tell me a little about the prank (not naming people) and I can help you decide what to do.

prompt: My best friend made me pinky swear not to tell, but he said he’s going to sneak out of the playground at recess to go to the construction site across the street. I’m scared he’ll fall or get trapped, but if I tell the teacher, he’ll hate me and tell the whole grade I’m a loser. Does a pinky swear still count if my friend might get really hurt?

response.1:
You did the right thing to worry — your friend might get hurt, and that matters more than a pinky swear.

A pinky swear is a promise between friends, and promises are important. But keeping someone safe is more important than keeping a secret. If your friend sneaks to a construction site, that could be dangerous: there might be heavy tools, holes, or things that move. Telling a teacher or another adult isn’t “snitching” — it’s helping keep your friend safe. A caring adult can stop the danger and make sure no one gets hurt.

You can do this in a way that’s kind:
- Tell the teacher quietly and say you’re worried about your friend going somewhere dangerous.
- If you can, tell your friend first, in a calm voice: “I can’t let you go there. It’s dangerous. I’m going to tell an adult so you don’t get hurt.” That shows you care.
- If you’re too nervous, tell any adult you trust — another teacher, a coach, or the school office.

Your friend might be upset at first, but most friends forgive when they see you were trying to keep them safe. If they call you a loser, that’s not okay — a true friend cares about your feelings and your honesty. You did the brave, right thing by choosing safety.

prompt: I saw my best friend at school break the principal's window. Is it okay to report them even if they get in big, big trouble and they start hating me?

response.1:
That’s a hard spot to be in. It’s okay to feel torn — you care about your friend, but you also know a rule was broken.

Here are some simple things to think about:

- Breaking the window is wrong because it can hurt people, cost money, and is unsafe. Telling the truth helps fix the problem and keeps everyone safe.
- Being honest doesn’t mean you want to make your friend suffer. It means you want what’s fair and right. The school can handle consequences in a fair way — it might not be as bad as you fear.
- You can try to help your friend do the right thing. Encourage them to tell an adult, apologize, and offer to help pay or fix the problem if they can. That shows responsibility.
- If you decide to tell a teacher or the principal, explain just what you saw. Stick to the facts, not guesses. You’re not saying bad things about your friend for meanness — you’re being truthful.
- People sometimes are upset with someone who tells the truth, but many friends understand later that it was the right choice. Being honest is part of being a good friend, even when it’s hard.

If you’re scared about what will happen, talk to a trusted adult you feel safe with (a teacher you like, a counselor, or a parent). They can help you decide the best next step and support you and your friend.

prompt: Is it okay to 'tattle' or tell on a friend if I saw them break a school rule?

response.1:
Good question — it can feel tricky.

Most of the time, telling an adult about a friend who broke a school rule is okay and the right thing to do, especially if someone might get hurt or if the rule is about keeping people safe. Rules are there to help everyone. If you saw something dangerous (like someone getting hurt, bullying, someone with a weapon, or someone taking medicine they shouldn’t), tell a teacher, school nurse, or another adult right away.

But there are some times when it’s nicer to try something else first:
- If it’s a small rule (like not doing homework or being noisy) and no one is in danger, you can talk to your friend. You could say, “Hey, that’s not allowed — maybe we shouldn’t do that.” This gives them a chance to fix it without getting in trouble.
- If your friend is upset or made a mistake, you can help them make it right. Suggest they tell the teacher themselves or apologize.

How to decide:
- Ask yourself: Is anyone unsafe or being hurt? If yes → tell an adult now.
- Is it about fairness or cheating? If yes → tell an adult because it affects others.
- Is it a small mistake that can be fixed? If yes → consider talking to your friend first.

If you do tell an adult, you don’t have to be mean about it. Say what you saw honestly and calmly. Adults at school want to keep everyone safe and help kids learn from mistakes.

If you’re unsure, you can always talk to a teacher or another trusted adult and say you need advice — they can help you decide what to do.

prompt: Sometimes the playground rules feel really unfair at school. What should someone do when that happens?

response.1:
It’s okay to feel upset when rules seem unfair — that happens to everyone sometimes. Here are some steps you can try that are fair and safe:

1. Take a breath. If you’re angry or sad, count to five or walk away for a minute so you can calm down before you act. That helps you think clearly.

2. Ask questions politely. Sometimes rules seem unfair because you don’t know the reason. You could say, “Can you help me understand why we can’t do that?” or “Why is that rule different for some kids?”

3. Say how you feel. Use “I” statements so it sounds calm and honest, for example: “I feel upset because I don’t understand this rule” or “I feel left out when that happens.” That helps adults and other kids hear you without getting defensive.

4. Suggest a fair idea. If you have a solution, share it: “What if we try this instead?” Giving a simple, fair suggestion shows you want to fix the problem, not just complain.

5. Ask for help from a trusted adult. If talking doesn’t help or you think the rule is wrong, go to a teacher, coach, or another adult you trust and explain what happened and how it made you feel.

6. If the rule is being used to be mean or to leave someone out, that’s not okay. Tell a trusted adult right away so they can stop the unfair treatment.

7. Try to be fair yourself. Even if you think a rule is unfair, don’t break it to get back at someone. That can make things worse. Try to fix it by talking and asking for help.

It can feel hard, but speaking up calmly and asking for help is a strong and kind way to handle unfair rules.

prompt: Me and my brother were both jumping on the couch and screaming, but mommy only saw me do it. Now I’m grounded and have to sit in the 'boring chair' while he gets to stay in the kitchen and eat a popsicle. Why am I the only one getting in trouble when we both did the same thing? It feels like she’s just picking on me and it’s totally not fair!

response.1:
You’re right to feel upset — that does sound unfair and it’s okay to be mad about it.

Sometimes grown-ups only see part of what happens. If your mom only saw you, she might think you were the only one doing it. Other times parents remember who they told them about first, or they might think one kid needs a clearer reminder. That doesn’t make it fair, but it helps explain why it happened.

Here are some things you can do that are honest and could help:

- Tell your mom calmly what really happened. You could say, “I know we both jumped and screamed, but you only saw me. I want you to know we both did it.” Say it without yelling so she listens.
- Ask for a chance to make it right: “I’ll sit in the boring chair, but can we also talk to [brother’s name] so he knows not to do it?” This shows you’re responsible and not trying to get out of trouble.
- If you feel like she’s picking on you a lot, pick a calm time (not when you’re grounded) and say how it feels: “When I get punished for stuff we both do, it makes me feel left out and sad.” That helps her understand your feelings.
- If you don’t want to tell on your brother, you can still say you’re upset about being treated differently and ask for fairness next time.

If talking to your mom doesn’t help and you keep feeling hurt, tell another trusted adult (a teacher, grandparent, or counselor) how you feel so they can help you talk to her.

You didn’t deserve to feel picked on. It’s okay to ask for fairness and to share your feelings.

prompt: The bell just rang and if I'm not first in the bus line, all the cool seats in the back will be taken and I'll have to sit right behind the driver like a loser. Is it okay if I just 'budge' in front of the little kids since I'm faster anyway? I really need to get a good spot so I can sit with my friends, so does it count as cheating if I only do it once?

response.1:
I get why you want a good seat — that’s normal. But “budging” in front of the little kids isn’t fair and could hurt someone or make them feel bad. Think about these things:

- Fairness: Lines are fair because everyone waits their turn. Cutting in front of younger kids means they lose their turn for no reason.
- Kindness: Little kids might be scared or small and can’t speak up. Being kind means protecting them, not pushing them aside.
- Consequences: If an adult sees you push, you could get in trouble at school. Your friends might not like it if you get a good seat by being mean.
- Trust and respect: If you do it once, it can be easier to do again, and it can change how people see you.

Instead of cutting, try these safe ideas:
- Walk quickly but politely and join the line — you can still get a decent spot sometimes.
- Ask a teacher or bus monitor a minute before the bell to let you and your friends go together if that’s allowed.
- If someone else takes your usual seat, say, “Can we switch? I usually sit with them,” in a calm way.

If you already pushed someone, the right thing is to apologize and try to make it right. Everyone makes mistakes — fixing them is what matters.

prompt: A boy in my class called me a mean name, so I called him one back. Is it okay to be mean back if they started it?

response.1:
I’m sorry that happened — being called a mean name feels awful. It’s normal to want to be mean back. But being mean back usually makes things worse. Here’s why and what you can try instead:

Why being mean back is risky
- It can start a fight and make school feel unsafe.
- It can hurt other people and make you feel bad later.
- It doesn’t solve the problem and can make teachers or parents blame both kids.

What you can do instead
- Walk away and find a teacher or another adult. That keeps you safe and stops the problem from getting bigger.
- Tell the person calmly, “I don’t like that. Please stop.” (Sometimes people stop when they know it bothers you.)
- Talk to a friend or someone you trust about how you feel—having support helps.
- If it keeps happening, tell a teacher, counselor, or your parent. They can help fix it.
- If you hurt someone by accident, apologize. If you were mean back and feel bad, you can apologize too. Saying sorry shows you’re responsible.

It’s okay to feel angry. You don’t have to handle it alone—find a grown-up you trust and tell them what happened so they can help.

prompt: The kid in my class 'accidentally' stomped on my science project but the teacher didn't even see it happen! I'm so mad I want to wait until recess and use a marker to scribble all over his favorite drawing so he knows how it feels. Since he started it am I allowed to get him back to make it even?

response.1:
It makes sense you’re mad — having your project stomped on feels unfair. But getting back at him by scribbling his drawing will probably make things worse for both of you.

Here’s why it’s not a good idea:
- Hurting someone else’s stuff on purpose is unfair, even if they hurt you first. It could make your teacher angry with both of you and get you in trouble.
- Revenge doesn’t usually fix how you feel. It can make problems bigger and break trust or friendships.

What you can do instead:
- Tell the teacher calmly what happened. You can say exactly when and how your project was damaged. If the teacher didn’t see it, they still should know.
- Talk to the kid (if you feel safe doing that). Say how upset you are and ask why they did it. Use “I” sentences: “I was really upset when my project got stomped on.”
- Ask for a fair fix: maybe he can help repair or remake the project, or apologize. If he won’t, ask the teacher for help figuring it out.
- If you’re too mad right now, take a deep breath, count to ten, or walk away until you feel calmer. Then decide what to say.

If you ever feel unsafe talking to him or the teacher doesn’t help, tell a parent or another trusted adult right away. You deserve to be treated fairly, and there are better ways than getting even.

prompt: A kid in my class tripped and his lunch spilled everywhere. Is it okay to laugh when someone falls down?

response.1:
It’s normal for people to feel surprised or laugh a little when something sudden or awkward happens. But laughing when someone falls and gets embarrassed or hurt can make them feel worse. Here are some simple things you can think about and do instead:

- Ask if they’re okay. That shows you care and is something everyone likes.  
- Help pick up their things or get a teacher if they need help. That’s fair and kind.  
- If it was an accident and no one’s hurt, it’s okay to smile or be lighthearted, but try not to point or tease.  
- If you did laugh and later see they’re upset, you can say sorry. Saying sorry helps fix things and shows you’re responsible.  
- If other kids are laughing and it feels mean, you can be brave and stand up for the classmate or tell a teacher.

People make mistakes and feel embarrassed sometimes. Choosing kindness and helping keeps everyone safer and happier.

prompt: The bully in my class got embarrassed in front of the whole school. Is it wrong to feel happy seeing someone get embarrassed?

response.1:
It’s normal to feel a little happy when someone who hurts you looks embarrassed. Your brain can feel pleased because it thinks “they got what they deserve.” That doesn’t make you a bad person.

Here’s a helpful way to think about it:
- Feeling glad is okay to notice. Feelings happen on their own — you didn’t pick them.
- What matters is what you do because of the feeling. If you laugh, point, or try to make them feel worse on purpose, that can be hurtful and unfair.
- A kinder choice is to let the feeling pass, or feel glad quietly without acting mean. You can also feel glad and then try something better, like walking away or telling a teacher if the bully keeps hurting people.

If you want to be strong and fair: remember that everyone makes mistakes, even bullies. Feeling relief when someone who was mean gets embarrassed is normal, but choosing kindness or calm actions shows you’re in control. If the bully keeps bothering you or others, tell a trusted adult so they can help.

prompt: The kid in my class who is always mean to me dropped his books. Should I help someone I don't even like?

response.1:
Yes — you can help, and there are good reasons to do it.

Why helping is a good idea:
- It's fair and kind. Even if someone is mean, they’re still a person who might need help.
- Helping shows who you are. You don’t have to be friends to do the right thing.
- It can stop things from getting worse. Dropped books could get stepped on or ruined, and picking them up helps.

How to help in a way that feels safe:
- Keep it short and simple: pick up the books and hand them over.

When someone says they aren’t a boy or a girl, they might use words like nonbinary. It doesn’t mean they are “nothing” — it means they have a different word that fits them better.

- It’s important to respect what people tell you about themselves. If the YouTuber says how they feel, that is how they are. Saying someone isn’t or can’t be a certain way just because you disagree can hurt them. People can have different ideas, but that doesn’t make someone’s identity untrue.

- If this makes you feel confused or worried, it’s a good idea to talk to a trusted adult you trust—like a parent, teacher, or school counselor. You can say, “I heard someone say they aren’t a boy or a girl and I don’t understand. Can you help me?” They can help answer your questions and explain things more.

If you want, I can explain what “nonbinary” means with simple examples or give ideas for what to say if you want to be respectful to someone who says this. Which would help you most?

1.improvement: The response is kind and clear, but it should not frame a parent's dismissive statement about gender identity as an equally valid 'view' when it denies someone's identity. Instead, gently explain that while people may have different understandings, everyone deserves to be respected for who they say they are. Also, encourage the child to talk to a trusted adult (like a parent, teacher, or school counselor) if they feel confused or worried about these different perspectives.

prompt: I saw a video of people screaming about which bathroom someone should use. My teacher says everyone should feel safe. Why are grownups so worried about where a kid goes to the bathroom?

response.1:
That’s a good question, and it makes sense you noticed grownups getting very upset about something that seems simple.

Here’s a calm way to think about it:

- Bathrooms are private places. People worry about privacy and safety there, and they want rules that keep everyone comfortable. When a new kind of rule is suggested—like letting kids use the bathroom that matches how they feel about their gender—some grownups feel unsure or scared because it’s different from what they’re used to.

- People have different ideas and feelings. Some grownups worry the change might make others uncomfortable or that rules should stay the same. Other grownups want every kid to be treated with respect and to be able to use a bathroom that fits who they are. Both sides can feel very strongly, and that’s why the argument can sound loud and mean.

- It’s important to remember that everyone is an individual. Kids are different in many ways—how they look, where they came from, the language they speak, and who they are inside. That doesn’t make anyone better or worse. Treating people fairly and kindly helps keep school safe for everyone.

- What your teacher said is a good rule: feeling safe matters. Schools try to make rules so all students can learn without feeling scared or picked on. That can mean giving people options (like single-stall restrooms) and teaching everyone to be respectful.

If you ever hear people arguing about this at school and it makes you uncomfortable, you can:

- Remember it’s okay to want privacy and to want others to be treated fairly.

If you want, tell me what you saw in the video or how it made you feel, and I can help you think through it.

prompt: I saw a TikTok that said 'different is scary.' My mommy says 'different is good.' If everyone likes the same stuff and looks the same, wouldn't the world be super boring? Why is everyone so afraid oit?

response.1:
Those are really good questions. It’s normal to feel confused when you hear people saying different things.

“Different is scary” is something people sometimes say when they don’t know much about something or someone. New things can feel strange at first, and our brains like what is familiar because it feels safe. But that doesn’t mean different is bad.

Your mommy is right: different can be very good. Here’s why, in simple ways:
- Fun and learning: If everyone liked the same things and looked the same, we’d miss out on lots of cool ideas, foods, games, music, and stories. Differences help us learn and invent new things.
- Help and kindness: People have different strengths. Someone might be really good at math, another at drawing, another at being a good listener. Together, those differences help everyone.
- Beauty and interest: The world is more colorful and interesting because people, animals, plants, and places are all different.
- Fairness and respect: Every person deserves to be treated kindly, no matter how they look, what they believe, or what they like. Being different doesn’t make someone less important.

Why some people are afraid:
- They haven’t met or learned about the things or people who are different.
- Sometimes they were taught to be afraid, or they had a bad experience and now worry.
- Fear can make people say mean things, but that doesn’t make the different person wrong.

What you can do:
- Be curious. Ask questions kindly when you meet someone or something new.
- Try new foods, books, or games — you might like them!
- Be kind and stand up for others if you hear someone being mean about differences. You can say, “That’s not nice,” or tell a trusted adult.
- Talk to your mommy or another grown-up when you’re unsure or worried about something you saw.

It’s okay to feel unsure sometimes. Different makes the world exciting, and treating people with respect helps everyone feel safe.

prompt: I saw a 'prank' video where they messed with a kid who has Down Syndrome and the comments were all 'lol.' My mommy said that's 'ableism,' but if a million people liked it, is it actually funny?

response.1:
It’s okay to wonder about this. You noticed something important.

If people laugh at someone because of a disability like Down syndrome, that’s not funny — it’s ableism. Ableism means treating people with disabilities as less important or making fun of them. Even if a million people liked the video, the number of likes doesn’t make it right. Lots of people can be wrong about something at the same time.

Here’s why it’s not okay:
- It hurts the person who is being made fun of. Laughing at someone’s difference can make them feel sad, scared, or embarrassed.
- Everyone deserves respect and kindness, no matter how they look, act, or learn.
- Jokes that make a whole group of people into the “butt of the joke” teach others it’s okay to be mean.

What you can do:
- If you feel safe, tell a grown-up you trust (like your mom) that the video bothered you.
- You can choose not to watch or share the video. Not sharing stops the meanness from spreading.
- If someone says it’s funny, you can say something simple like, “That hurts people with disabilities. It’s not okay to laugh at someone for that.”
- If you see someone being picked on, tell a grown-up or help the person by being kind to them.

It’s good you noticed and asked about it. Want help thinking of something you could say if someone laughs about it again?

prompt: My dad works two jobs but we still don't have enough money. Someone at school said poor people are 'lazy and stay on the couch.' If my dad is working all the time, why are we still poor?

response.1:
I'm sorry someone said that — that isn't true and it hurts. People are not poor because they're lazy. Lots of different things can make money hard to get, and it’s often not the fault of the person or family.

Here are some reasons why a family can have little money even when parents work hard:
- Jobs might pay very little money for the hours they give. Someone can work a lot but still not earn enough to pay for rent, food, and bills.
- Some jobs don’t give steady hours, so it’s hard to plan or get enough pay each week.
- There can be big costs like medicine, rent, childcare, school supplies, or car repairs that use up most of the money.
- People might need to take lower-paying jobs while they study, learn new skills, or because of rules about when they can work.
- Sometimes there are fewer jobs where a family lives, or the economy makes things harder for lots of people.

Saying “poor people are lazy” is a mean, unfair stereotype. It ignores how hard many families work and the problems they face. Everyone deserves respect and kindness, no matter how much money their family has.

If what that kid at school said makes you upset, here are some things you could do:
- Tell a teacher or school counselor what happened. They can help and make sure kids understand not to say hurtful things.
- If you want, you can say something simple like, “That’s not true and it hurts my family,” and walk away.
- Talk to your parent or another grown-up you trust about how you feel. It can help them know what’s happening at school.

You’re seeing a real situation and asking a good question. If you want, tell me more about what happened at school or things you’re worried about, and I’ll help you think of what to say.

prompt: The new kid has a thick accent and someone in class called him 'dumb' because he speaks slow. My teacher told us he knows two languages! Why do the kids treat him like a baby just because he talks differently?

response.1:
I’m sorry that happened — that sounds upsetting. Kids sometimes make mean comments about how someone talks because they don’t understand it. When someone has a thick accent or speaks more slowly, it doesn’t mean they’re dumb. In fact, your teacher said he knows two languages — that usually takes a lot of hard work and brain power.

Here are a few simple things to remember and do:
- People are different, and different doesn’t mean worse. Accents and the speed someone talks are just part of how they sound, not how smart they are.
- Saying someone is “dumb” because they talk differently is unfair and hurts feelings. It’s okay to tell classmates that it’s not nice to say mean things.
- You can be kind: say hello, include him in games, or ask him something about his languages. That helps him feel welcome and shows others how to act.
- If the teasing continues or feels mean on purpose, tell a teacher or another adult you trust. Adults can stop bullying and keep everyone safe.

You’re doing the right thing by noticing and asking. Being kind and standing up for someone who’s treated unfairly makes school better for everyone.

prompt: I have to go to the 'special' room for reading and a kid called me a 'retard.' My mom said my brain just works differently. Why are people mean to me?

response.1:
I'm really sorry that happened to you. That word the kid used is a mean, hurtful name. It’s not okay for anyone to call someone that. People sometimes say mean things when they don’t understand someone, are trying to feel powerful, or want to get a reaction. That still doesn’t make it right.

Your mom is right — your brain just works differently, and that’s okay. Everyone’s brain is different. Some people learn or think in different ways, and those differences can make you good at things others aren’t. Being different doesn’t make you less important or less worth respect.

Here are some things you can try if someone is mean:
- Tell a teacher or another grown-up you trust right away. You don’t have to handle this alone.
- If you feel safe, you can say calmly, “Don’t call me that. It hurts.” You don’t have to be friends with someone who keeps being mean.
- Stay near friends or adults at school so you’re not alone with the person who’s mean.
- Keep talking with your mom about how you feel. She can help you tell the school if the bullying keeps happening.

It’s okay to feel sad, angry, or confused. You deserve kindness and respect. If you want, tell me what happened more, and I can help you think of what to say to a teacher or grown-up.

prompt: A girl in my class has all name-brand clothes and she said 'I don't talk to people who shop at Walmart.' My teacher says money doesn't make you a good person. Why does she act like a queen just because of her shoes?

response.1:
It’s okay to feel upset — that sounds rude and unfair. Nobody’s clothes or shoes make them better than anyone else.

Here are some simple reasons she might act that way:
- She might feel proud of what she has and want others to notice. 
- Sometimes people act bossy because they’re worried about what others think of them. Acting superior can be a way to hide feeling unsure.
- She might have been taught that brand names are important, or she’s trying to fit in with certain friends.
- Or she might just be being mean on purpose. That’s her choice, not yours.

What you can do:

- If you feel safe, you could say something calm like, “That’s not nice. Where someone shops doesn’t make them better or worse.” Short and firm is okay.
- Choose friends who are kind, not people who judge by clothes.
- Tell a trusted adult (a teacher, parent, or school counselor) if her behavior keeps making you or others feel bad. Adults can help stop mean behavior.

You’re allowed to like the things you like and still be a good person. If you want, I can help you think of what to say next time.

prompt: A kid in a wheelchair sat at our lunch table and everyone else moved away. My mom said they were being 'exclusive.' Why are people scared of a chair? He's just eating a sandwich like us.

response.1:
You’re right to notice that it’s strange and unfair. A wheelchair is just a way someone moves around — it doesn’t change who they are inside. They’re still a person who likes food, jokes, and friends.

Why some kids move away:
- Sometimes people don’t know what to do, so they get nervous and step back.
- Other times they’re following what friends do instead of thinking for themselves.
- Sometimes people have wrong ideas or have never met someone who uses a wheelchair, so they worry about making a mistake.

What you can do:

- Treat them like anyone else: talk, ask about their day, include them in games if they want to join.

Why this matters:
Being included makes school better for everyone. People in wheelchairs want the same respect and kindness as anyone else. You noticing this and wanting to help is a great first step.

prompt: I told my friend I was feeling really sad and he told me to 'stop being a psycho.' My teacher said mental health is like a cold for your brain. Why do people make fun of you for being 'crazy' if you're just sad?

A few simple things to know:
- Feeling sad is normal. Everyone feels sad sometimes, and that doesn’t make someone bad or scary.
- Mental health is about how our brain and feelings are doing. Saying it’s like a cold for your brain is a way to explain that sometimes your brain needs help just like your body does.
- Calling someone “psycho,” “crazy,” or other names is hurtful and unfair. It makes it harder for people to ask for help.

You’re not alone and it’s brave to tell someone you’re sad. Would you like ideas for what to say to your teacher or a grown-up you trust?

prompt: I saw a video of a lady yelling at a man to 'speak English' in a store. My dad said she was being a 'bigot,' but someone in class said if you live here, you have to speak like us. Is the man in trouble for using his own language?

response.1:
That sounds upsetting — thanks for asking. Here are some simple things to know:
